lessons.title: What is Recursion
lessons.concept: Recursion is a technique where a function solves a problem by calling itself on smaller subproblems. A correct recursive solution must define a base case (to stop recursion) and a recursive case (to reduce the problem toward the base case).
lessons.formula: Recursive solution = base case(s) + recursive case(s) that progress toward base case.
lessons.worked_example: Factorial: n! = 1 if n == 0 (base case), else n! = n * (n-1)! (recursive case). factorial(3) = 3 * factorial(2) = 3 * 2 * factorial(1) = 3 * 2 * 1 * factorial(0) = 6.
mistakes: Missing or incorrect base case causing infinite recursion/stack overflow
Recursive step that does not move toward the base case
Confusing the order of work done before and after the recursive call

lessons.title: Call Stack and Tracing Recursion
lessons.concept: Each recursive call creates a new stack frame storing parameters and local state. Calls are resolved in last-in, first-out (LIFO) order. Tracing recursion involves following calls down to the base case and then combining results as calls return.
lessons.formula: Execution: push frames until base case -> return values unwind stack in reverse call order.
lessons.worked_example: For factorial(3): calls stack as fact(3)->fact(2)->fact(1)->fact(0). fact(0) returns 1, fact(1) returns 1, fact(2) returns 2, fact(3) returns 6.
mistakes: Assuming all recursive calls run in parallel (they are sequential with stack frames)
Losing track of which instance of variables belongs to which call
Expecting the first call to finish before deeper calls are made

lessons.title: Time and Space in Recursion
lessons.concept: Recursive time complexity depends on number of calls and work per call. Space complexity includes recursion stack depth in addition to any extra data structures. Some naive recursions (like Fibonacci) recompute subproblems, leading to exponential time.
lessons.formula: Total time ~ (number of recursive calls) * (work per call). Stack space ~ maximum recursion depth.
lessons.worked_example: factorial(n) makes n+1 calls total with O(1) work each -> O(n) time and O(n) stack space. Naive Fibonacci fib(n)=fib(n-1)+fib(n-2) makes many repeated calls -> exponential time, with O(n) max depth.
mistakes: Counting only the first call and ignoring recursive subcalls
Forgetting stack space in space complexity analysis
Assuming recursion is always slower/worse without considering problem structure

practice.question: In which order do recursive call stack frames complete/return?
practice.explanation: The call stack is LIFO: the most recent (deepest) call returns first, then control returns to the previous call.

practice.explanation: There are about n+1 calls total and each does constant work, so total time is O(n).

practice.question: What happens if a recursive function has no base case (or never reaches it)?

options.C: It may recurse indefinitely until stack/resources are exhausted
options.D: It automatically converts to a loop

practice.explanation: Without a reachable base case, recursive calls continue without stopping, typically leading to infinite recursion and a stack overflow or resource exhaustion.

questions.question: For a recursive function that calls itself twice per invocation (e.g., naive Fibonacci) without memoization, the time complexity is typically:
questions.explanation: Each call branches into two more calls and subproblems are recomputed, leading to an exponential number of calls in the naive form (commonly expressed as O(2^n)).

questions.explanation: factorial(n) calls factorial(n-1), ..., factorial(0), so at most n+1 frames are on the stack at once, which is O(n) space.
